summary: Defines the audio/L16 MIME type, a reasonable-quality audio format for use in Internet applications. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This gives a name to a plain, uncompressed type of sound recording so programs know how to play it.

questions: what is audio l16 mime type
how to send uncompressed audio over internet
subtitle: A simple, uncompressed audio format for the internet

tldr.problem: Internet applications needed a standard way to transmit reasonable-quality audio without compression, but the only existing MIME audio types used low sampling rates that obscure speech.
tldr.mechanism: The audio/L16 type registers uncompressed, linearly-encoded audio at higher sample rates (up to 48 kHz) with support for multiple channels, following the format already used for RTP transport.
tldr.outcome: This informational RFC provides a standard name and parameters for audio applications to exchange high-quality speech and audio data over internet protocols like email and web uploads.

facts.label: Encoding
facts.value: Signed, two's complement, network byte order

today: RFC 2586 is an Informational RFC published in May 1999 and has not been obsoleted. The audio/L16 MIME type remains a straightforward option for applications that need uncompressed audio, though modern applications often prefer compressed formats for bandwidth efficiency.

sections.title: Introduction and Need
sections.content:
RFC 2586 defines audio/L16, a MIME type for uncompressed audio in internet applications. The RFC notes that existing MIME audio standards (audio/basic and audio/32kadpcm) operate at only 8000 samples per second, which is too low for advanced speech recognition and educational applications. This standard fills the gap by registering a simple MIME type that allows higher-rate, linear-encoded audio with multiple channels.

The motivation is practical: applications handling speech and voice need better quality than 8 kHz sampling provides, and they need a standard way to label and transmit such audio.
sections.plainLanguage: Old phone-quality audio (8000 samples per second) loses important sounds. This standard lets programs send better-quality voice over the internet without squeezing it down first.

sections.title: The Audio/L16 Format
sections.content:
Audio/L16 is based on the L16 format described in RFC 1890. The audio data uses 16-bit signed representation in two's complement notation with network byte order, making it simple to implement and compatible with WAV and AIFF audio formats.

The MIME type is parametrized by sample rate and channels. Standardized sample rates are 8000, 11025, 16000, 22050, 24000, 32000, 44100, and 48000 samples per second. The channels parameter defaults to 1 (mono) but can specify stereo (2) or more. When multiple channels are used, samples from each channel are interleaved, with lower-numbered channels preceding higher-numbered ones.
sections.plainLanguage: The format is a straightforward chain of numbers that represent the sound at regular time intervals. You specify how many times per second the samples come and how many speakers (channels) there are.

sections.title: IANA Registration and Usage
sections.content:
The RFC provides the formal IANA registration for the audio/L16 MIME type. The required parameters are rate (samples per second) and the optional channels parameter. The encoding is suitable for binary transport, and for email it should be base64-encoded since audio data is binary.

The type is compatible with WAV (Microsoft Windows RIFF) and Apple AIFF formats, as well as public domain programs like 'sox' and 'rateconv'. The intended usage is marked as 'Common,' reflecting the expectation that many audio and speech applications will use it.
sections.plainLanguage: The standard gives official names for the type and its settings, making it easy for email programs and websites to know they are handling sound correctly.

sections.title: Security Notes
sections.content: The RFC notes that audio data itself is believed to offer no security risks. However, it acknowledges that the format is well-suited for hiding data using steganography (concealing information within the audio), so implementers should be aware of that possibility in secure environments.
sections.plainLanguage: Audio files don't have built-in dangers, but someone could sneakily hide secret messages inside the sound.

references.text: Schulzrinne, H., "RTP Profile for Audio and Video Conferences with Minimal Control", RFC 1890, January 1996.
